title: 30 Years of RFCs
summary: Marks the 30th anniversary of the RFC series with a recollection from the then RFC Editor Joyce K. Reynolds, followed by recollections from pioneers Steve Crocker, who wrote RFC 1, Vint Cerf and Jake Feinler. It is informational and was later updated by RFC 8700.

eli5.summary: This is a birthday card for the RFC series, with stories from some of the people who started it.

questions: when was the first rfc published
subtitle: A thirtieth-anniversary tribute to the RFC series, told by people who helped create and run it.

tldr.problem: The RFC series reached its thirtieth anniversary in 1999, shortly after the death of its long-time editor Jon Postel, and its founders wanted to record how it began.
tldr.mechanism: The memo collects short recollections from Robert Braden, the then RFC Editor Joyce K. Reynolds, Steve Crocker, Vint Cerf and Jake Feinler, and ends with a call for votes on favorite RFCs.
tldr.outcome: It is a commemorative Informational memo with no technical specification, and it was later updated by RFC 8700.

facts.label: First four ARPANET sites
facts.value: UCLA, SRI, UC Santa Barbara, Utah

today: RFC 2555 is an Informational, commemorative memo and has not been obsoleted, but it is updated by RFC 8700. It records the series as it stood in 1999.

sections.title: A Tribute in Five Voices
sections.content:
RFC 2555 marks thirty years since RFC 1 was published at UCLA. The series then held more than 2500 documents on computer networking, collected, archived and edited by Jon Postel for 28 years. Postel had died, and the memo is offered in admiration for his contribution.

After Robert Braden's introduction, it holds recollections from the then RFC Editor Joyce K. Reynolds, and from three pioneers: Steve Crocker, who wrote RFC 1, Vint Cerf, and Jake Feinler.
sections.eli5: A few friends each tell a short story about how a very long-lived series of notes got started and who took care of it.

sections.title: Reynolds: Jon Postel Lets Go
sections.content:
Joyce K. Reynolds recalls working with Postel on IP network number and protocol parameter assignments. She noticed a pile of folders on his desk that grew into two stacks: documents waiting for RFC publication. When she suggested he hand off some work, he wheeled a computer stand of those documents into her office and said, "I'm letting go!"

On top was the "NLS Textbook" prepared at ISI for the TENEX and TOPS-20 systems. NLS was the system Postel used to write, edit and create the RFCs. Reynolds stresses his perseverance about consistent RFC style and quality.
sections.eli5: The editor had so many papers piled up that he finally handed a big stack to a colleague with a grin, and she learned the job.

sections.title: Crocker: The First Pebble
sections.content:
Steve Crocker describes RFC 1, "Host Software", issued on April 7, 1969, as a modest and entirely forgettable memo that was part of a broad initiative. The ARPANET was still being designed. BBN had won the contract for the Interface Message Processors (IMPs), the forerunners of the modern routers. The first four nodes were to be at UCLA, SRI, the University of California, Santa Barbara and the University of Utah.

A handful of graduate students and staff from those sites met in the summer of 1968. Their early thinking centered on applications and included downloading a small interpretive program at the start of a session, as in the Decode-Encode Language (DEL) of RFC 5 and the Network Interchange Language (NIL) of RFC 51.

Crocker says two lasting choices were an open architecture of multiple protocol layers and a deliberately informal tone. He took on the job of numbering and distributing the notes, and wanted them to be the start of a dialog and not an assertion of control. He believed the series would die off within a year or so.
sections.eli5: A few students were asked to figure out how computers could talk. They wrote friendly notes to each other, numbered them, and never guessed the notes would keep going for decades.

sections.title: Cerf: The Great Conversation
sections.content:
Vint Cerf traces how RFCs changed from tentative dialog to more structured documents as the Internet gained economic importance. He thanks four people in particular: Steve Crocker, Jon Postel, Joyce K. Reynolds and Bob Braden. He credits Postel's insistence on quality, notes that Reynolds assigned number 2468 to the RFC written to remember Postel, and points to Braden's work on RFC 1122 and RFC 1123.

He notes that Postel permitted material beyond purely technical documents, so the series includes poetry, humor (especially the April 1 RFCs) and reprinted reference material.

Several parallel note series, including Internet Experiment Notes (IENs), existed in the early 1970s. After the Internet protocols were mandated on the ARPANET and other DARPA-sponsored networks in January 1983, Internet-related notes were merged into the RFC series. Cerf agrees with Danny Cohen that a single series is easier to maintain and search. He also describes the IETF's growth into the dominant Internet standards body under the Internet Society, and the rise of Internet Drafts.
sections.eli5: Over time the notes went from friendly chats to careful official documents, and the people who edited them worked hard to keep them good.

sections.title: Feinler: The NIC and the First Few RFCs
sections.content:
Jake Feinler recounts that RFC 1 appeared on April 7, 1969 and RFC 2, by Bill Duvall of SRI, on April 9, 1969, and that Crocker's RFC 3, "Documentation Conventions", set the ground rules. RFC 3 said notes may be produced at any site by anybody, are encouraged to be timely rather than polished, and have a minimum length of one sentence.

She describes the SRI NLS Journal, an online bibliographic service where a search hit came with a "link" you could jump to for the full text, and where submitted documents could not be changed, only superseded by new versions. She became Principal Investigator for the NIC project in 1972, and the NIC distributed documents such as the Protocol Handbook.

She recalls that none of the RFCs were ever restricted or classified, even though funded by the DoD. In March 1982 a military directive made TCP and IP mandatory for DoD communications networks, which together with RFC 791 and RFC 793 gave the RFCs worldwide stature. When she left in 1989 there were about 30,000 hosts and just over 1000 RFCs.
sections.eli5: The earliest notes set simple rules: anyone can write one, it can be short, and it does not have to be perfect. That kept people sharing ideas freely.

sections.title: Favorite RFCs and Closing Notes
sections.content:
Celeste Anderson explains that she and Postel had hoped to mark the 25th anniversary with a book, and later planned to collect thirty "RFC Editors' Choice" RFCs for the thirtieth. Postel's death in October 1998 interrupted this. The memo invites votes on "Favorite RFCs -- The First 30 Years" for a book, with voting closing December 31, 1999.

The online versions of early RFCs, including RFC 1, were converted with some adjustments, and hand-drawn diagrams had to be turned into ASCII.

The memo's security section states that security issues are not discussed in this commemorative RFC.
sections.eli5: The authors asked readers to vote for their favorite notes so the best ones could be put in a book in Jon's memory.
